newsitem.title: USA: White House, Congress seek to avoid money dispute.
newsitem.headline: White House, Congress seek to avoid money dispute.

text.p: White House officials and senior members of Congress said Monday they were optimistic significant differences on defense and domestic spending can be worked out to avoid a pre-election government shutdown.
But White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta said the administration will insist on lower spending for defense than Republicans have proposed as a way to pay for additional education funding.

Both the White House and Republican leaders are under pressure to resolve a massive package of 13 separate appropriations bills before the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year. Without secure funding, some federal agencies could be forced into a politically embarrassing shutdown in the month before the election.

Amid speculation that the Republican party could lose control of the House, its leaders also hope they will resolve the issue so that Congress can adjourn for the year. That way their members can begin campaigning for re-election by the end of September.
Threats of a partial government shutdown would serve to remind voters of the two shutdowns last winter which were blamed on Republican intransigence in budget negotiations.

Panetta and President Clinton's new budget director Franklin Raines took the administration's request for increased domestic spending to a Capitol meeting with Republican and Democratic leaders of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees.
"Our concern is always to ensure that the investments we care about, particularly education is funded at levels preserving our continuing commitment to education," Panetta told reporters.
The Republican-led Congress is working on a $245 billion defense budget for 1997 that is about $10 billion above the president's request. Clinton would like to use some of this to fund education.

"A compromise is doable," House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston, R-Louisiana, told reporters after the closed meeting. But he disagreed with Clinton's belief that Republicans have underfunded education. "Education is level funded. What they are asking for are new initiatives, new money in education," he said.
